images.caption: Banganga Tank at Walkeshwar, February 2023. The rectangular stone talao, fed by a freshwater spring a few hundred metres from the Arabian Sea, is the oldest surviving element of the islands' pre-pipe water system - tradition ties the site to the Silhara dynasty of the twelfth century.
images.processing: Downsized to 2000px wide, JPEG quality 82, via macOS sips. No edits to image content.

images.caption: Murphy's map of the Island of Bombay and Colaba, 1843 - the seven islands two generations after the Hornby Vellard fused them. The low 'Flats' behind the causeway, drawn here as open ground, are the bowl the city later built over: the land that drowned on 26 July 2005.
images.credit: From Materials Towards a Statistical Account of the Town and Island of Bombay, 1843 (public domain).
images.processing: Converted PNG to JPEG at 1400px wide, quality 80, via macOS sips. No edits to image content.

images.caption: Vihar Lake from Yogi Hills, with the towers of Mulund behind, 2025. The reservoir that gave Bombay its first piped water in 1860 still sits inside the city that outgrew it - today it supplies about 90 of Mumbai's roughly 4,000 MLD.
images.processing: Downsized to 2000px wide, JPEG quality 82, via macOS sips. No edits to image content.

images.caption: The Vaitarna system near Igatpuri, monsoon 2016. The river's dams - Modak Sagar (1957), Upper Vaitarna (1973), Middle Vaitarna (2014) - mark the city's long walk into the Western Ghats, each one pushing the source farther from the tap.

images.caption: A state transport bus abandoned near the Western Express Highway flyover at Borivali, 28 July 2005 - two days after the Santacruz observatory recorded 944 mm of rain in twenty-four hours.
